During large geomagnetic storms, red auroras are typically observed from low-latitude countries such 
as Japan. The color arises from a specific emission line of oxygen atoms at high altitudes. However, 
during the May 10-11th 2024 superstorm, magenta auroras were observed above Japan instead of 
the typical red. In this study, we demonstrate that the magenta hue is created by a mixture of red 
(O) and a blue (N
2
+) aurora at extremely high altitudes. The blue color originates from the N
2
+ first 
negative emission band caused by both resonant scattering of the upwelling molecular ions and heavy 
particle precipitation during the storm. This study is primarily driven by observations from citizen 
scientists, and confirmed and quantified with observations from spacecraft and modeling techniques. 
Additionally, we show that high solar activity, terrestrial season, and the preheating of the atmosphere 
all contribute to the occurrence of magenta aurora. This study showcases the value and richness of 
citizen science, and we anticipate that such approaches will become increasingly important in the 
future.
In early May 2024, a series of solar flares and subsequent coronal mass ejections (CME) triggered an extreme 
geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic 
Observatory and 6th in the 66-year history of the Dst index. This super storm caused aurora to appear above lo
latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time 
auroral observations on social media platforms such as X. In Japan alone, over a thousand people attempted to
view the aurora, leading to one of the densest observation efforts in the world. The public used commercially 
available cameras to capture the faint auroras that were mostly invisible to the naked eye. Remarkably, the 
photographs reveal a clear and dominant magenta hue instead of the traditional red typically observed above 
Japan3,4 (Fig. 1). This study aims to investigate the cause of this magenta aurora through photographs from the 
public, spacecraft observations, and physics-based and statistical modeling.
Utilizing citizen scientists to observe the aurora is a powerful and relatively recent advance in our field
8,9. 
Such an approach was used to quantify the unusually bright auroras observed during the December 1st 2023 
storm10, which was confined to the northernmost parts of Japan, with an order of 10·s of citizen observations. 
During the May 10-11th 2024 storm, 100·s of citizen observations were made across the full length of Japan 
(Method). To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest number of auroral sightings above Japan during a 
single event.
The background and the time sequence of events is as follows: from May 7th an unprecedented 5, and 
possibly more, halo CMEs left the Sun and headed towards Earth. After reaching Earth on May 10th, an extrem
geomagnetic storm was triggered. The storm peaked at 0200 UT (1100 Japan Standard Time) on May 11th wit
the real-time Dst index of -412 nT. This was the largest storm since the 2003 Halloween storms. When combine
with a favorable local time and slow recovery phase; this provided Japan with the right conditions to observe 
the aurorae11. The solar wind parameters, storm evolution, and citizen science observations are illustrated in

latitude (GLAT). Extended Data Figure 2 shows the total number of observation attempts (775), with ·Yes· 
indicating success and ·No· meaning unsuccessful. The time variation of the citizen observations is shown in

During large geomagnetic storms, red auroras are typically observed from low-latitude countries such 
as Japan. The color arises from a specific emission line of oxygen atoms at high altitudes. However, 
during the May 10-11th 2024 superstorm, magenta auroras were observed above Japan instead of 
the typical red. In this study, we demonstrate that the magenta hue is created by a mixture of red 
(O) and a blue (N
2

+ first 
negative emission band caused by both resonant scattering of the upwelling molecular ions and heavy 
particle precipitation during the storm. This study is primarily driven by observations from citizen 
scientists, and confirmed and quantified with observations from spacecraft and modeling techniques. 
Additionally, we show that high solar activity, terrestrial season, and the preheating of the atmosphere 
all contribute to the occurrence of magenta aurora. This study showcases the value and richness of 
citizen science, and we anticipate that such approaches will become increasingly important in the

In early May 2024, a series of solar flares and subsequent coronal mass ejections (CME) triggered an extreme 
geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic 
Observatory and 6th in the 66-year history of the Dst index. This super storm caused aurora to appear above lo
latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time 
auroral observations on social media platforms such as X. In Japan alone, over a thousand people attempted to
view the aurora, leading to one of the densest observation efforts in the world. The public used commercially 
available cameras to capture the faint auroras that were mostly invisible to the naked eye. Remarkably, the 
photographs reveal a clear and dominant magenta hue instead of the traditional red typically observed above 
Japan3,4 (Fig. 1). This study aims to investigate the cause of this magenta aurora through photographs from the 
public, spacecraft observations, and physics-based and statistical modeling.
Utilizing citizen scientists to observe the aurora is a powerful and relatively recent advance in our field
8,9. 
Such an approach was used to quantify the unusually bright auroras observed during the December 1st 2023 
storm10, which was confined to the northernmost parts of Japan, with an order of 10·s of citizen observations. 
During the May 10-11th 2024 storm, 100·s of citizen observations were made across the full length of Japan 
(Method). To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest number of auroral sightings above Japan during a 
single event.

during the May 10-11th 2024 superstorm, magenta auroras were observed above Japan instead of 
the typical red. In this study, we demonstrate that the magenta hue is created by a mixture of red 
(O) and a blue (N
2
+) aurora at extremely high altitudes. The blue color originates from the N
2
+ first 
negative emission band caused by both resonant scattering of the upwelling molecular ions and heavy 
particle precipitation during the storm. This study is primarily driven by observations from citizen 
scientists, and confirmed and quantified with observations from spacecraft and modeling techniques. 
Additionally, we show that high solar activity, terrestrial season, and the preheating of the atmosphere 
all contribute to the occurrence of magenta aurora. This study showcases the value and richness of 
citizen science, and we anticipate that such approaches will become increasingly important in the 
future.
In early May 2024, a series of solar flares and subsequent coronal mass ejections (CME) triggered an extreme 
geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic 
Observatory and 6th in the 66-year history of the Dst index. This super storm caused aurora to appear above lo
latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time 
auroral observations on social media platforms such as X. In Japan alone, over a thousand people attempted to
view the aurora, leading to one of the densest observation efforts in the world. The public used commercially 
available cameras to capture the faint auroras that were mostly invisible to the naked eye. Remarkably, the 
photographs reveal a clear and dominant magenta hue instead of the traditional red typically observed above 
Japan3,4 (Fig. 1). This study aims to investigate the cause of this magenta aurora through photographs from the 
public, spacecraft observations, and physics-based and statistical modeling.
Utilizing citizen scientists to observe the aurora is a powerful and relatively recent advance in our field
8,9. 
Such an approach was used to quantify the unusually bright auroras observed during the December 1st 2023 
storm10, which was confined to the northernmost parts of Japan, with an order of 10·s of citizen observations. 
During the May 10-11th 2024 storm, 100·s of citizen observations were made across the full length of Japan 
(Method). To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest number of auroral sightings above Japan during a 
single event.
The background and the time sequence of events is as follows: from May 7th an unprecedented 5, and 
possibly more, halo CMEs left the Sun and headed towards Earth. After reaching Earth on May 10th, an extrem
geomagnetic storm was triggered. The storm peaked at 0200 UT (1100 Japan Standard Time) on May 11th wit
the real-time Dst index of -412 nT. This was the largest storm since the 2003 Halloween storms. When combine
with a favorable local time and slow recovery phase; this provided Japan with the right conditions to observe 
the aurorae11. The solar wind parameters, storm evolution, and citizen science observations are illustrated in 
Extended Data Figure 1.

In early May 2024, a series of solar flares and subsequent coronal mass ejections (CME) triggered an extreme 
geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic

latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time

view the aurora, leading to one of the densest observation efforts in the world. The public used commercially 
available cameras to capture the faint auroras that were mostly invisible to the naked eye. Remarkably, the 
photographs reveal a clear and dominant magenta hue instead of the traditional red typically observed above 
Japan3,4 (Fig. 1). This study aims to investigate the cause of this magenta aurora through photographs from the 
public, spacecraft observations, and physics-based and statistical modeling.

8,9.

(Method). To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest number of auroral sightings above Japan during a 
single event.

possibly more, halo CMEs left the Sun and headed towards Earth. After reaching Earth on May 10th, an extrem
geomagnetic storm was triggered. The storm peaked at 0200 UT (1100 Japan Standard Time) on May 11th wit
the real-time Dst index of -412 nT. This was the largest storm since the 2003 Halloween storms. When combine

In early May 2024, a series of solar flares and subsequent coronal mass ejections (CME) triggered an extreme 
geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic

latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time 
auroral observations on social media platforms such as X. In Japan alone, over a thousand people attempted to
view the aurora, leading to one of the densest observation efforts in the world. The public used commercially 
available cameras to capture the faint auroras that were mostly invisible to the naked eye. Remarkably, the

During large geomagnetic storms, red auroras are typically observed from low-latitude countries such 
as Japan. The color arises from a specific emission line of oxygen atoms at high altitudes. However, 
during the May 10-11th 2024 superstorm, magenta auroras were observed above Japan instead of 
the typical red. In this study, we demonstrate that the magenta hue is created by a mixture of red 
(O) and a blue (N
2
+) aurora at extremely high altitudes. The blue color originates from the N
2
+ first 
negative emission band caused by both resonant scattering of the upwelling molecular ions and heavy 
particle precipitation during the storm. This study is primarily driven by observations from citizen 
scientists, and confirmed and quantified with observations from spacecraft and modeling techniques. 
Additionally, we show that high solar activity, terrestrial season, and the preheating of the atmosphere 
all contribute to the occurrence of magenta aurora. This study showcases the value and richness of 
citizen science, and we anticipate that such approaches will become increasingly important in the 
future.
In early May 2024, a series of solar flares and subsequent coronal mass ejections (CME) triggered an extreme 
geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic 
Observatory and 6th in the 66-year history of the Dst index. This super storm caused aurora to appear above lo
latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time 
auroral observations on social media platforms such as X. In Japan alone, over a thousand people attempted to
view the aurora, leading to one of the densest observation efforts in the world. The public used commercially 
available cameras to capture the faint auroras that were mostly invisible to the naked eye. Remarkably, the 
photographs reveal a clear and dominant magenta hue instead of the traditional red typically observed above 
Japan3,4 (Fig. 1). This study aims to investigate the cause of this magenta aurora through photographs from the 
public, spacecraft observations, and physics-based and statistical modeling.
Utilizing citizen scientists to observe the aurora is a powerful and relatively recent advance in our field
8,9. 
Such an approach was used to quantify the unusually bright auroras observed during the December 1st 2023 
storm10, which was confined to the northernmost parts of Japan, with an order of 10·s of citizen observations. 
During the May 10-11th 2024 storm, 100·s of citizen observations were made across the full length of Japan 
(Method). To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest number of auroral sightings above Japan during a 
single event.
The background and the time sequence of events is as follows: from May 7th an unprecedented 5, and 
possibly more, halo CMEs left the Sun and headed towards Earth. After reaching Earth on May 10th, an extrem
geomagnetic storm was triggered. The storm peaked at 0200 UT (1100 Japan Standard Time) on May 11th wit
the real-time Dst index of -412 nT. This was the largest storm since the 2003 Halloween storms. When combine
with a favorable local time and slow recovery phase; this provided Japan with the right conditions to observe 
the aurorae11. The solar wind parameters, storm evolution, and citizen science observations are illustrated in

indicating success and ·No· meaning unsuccessful. The time variation of the citizen observations is shown in

During large geomagnetic storms, red auroras are typically observed from low-latitude countries such 
as Japan. The color arises from a specific emission line of oxygen atoms at high altitudes. However, 
during the May 10-11th 2024 superstorm, magenta auroras were observed above Japan instead of 
the typical red. In this study, we demonstrate that the magenta hue is created by a mixture of red 
(O) and a blue (N
2
+) aurora at extremely high altitudes. The blue color originates from the N
2
+ first 
negative emission band caused by both resonant scattering of the upwelling molecular ions and heavy 
particle precipitation during the storm. This study is primarily driven by observations from citizen 
scientists, and confirmed and quantified with observations from spacecraft and modeling techniques. 
Additionally, we show that high solar activity, terrestrial season, and the preheating of the atmosphere 
all contribute to the occurrence of magenta aurora. This study showcases the value and richness of 
citizen science, and we anticipate that such approaches will become increasingly important in the 
future.
In early May 2024, a series of solar flares and subsequent coronal mass ejections (CME) triggered an extreme 
geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic 
Observatory and 6th in the 66-year history of the Dst index. This super storm caused aurora to appear above lo
latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time 
auroral observations on social media platforms such as X. In Japan alone, over a thousand people attempted to
view the aurora, leading to one of the densest observation efforts in the world. The public used commercially 
available cameras to capture the faint auroras that were mostly invisible to the naked eye. Remarkably, the 
photographs reveal a clear and dominant magenta hue instead of the traditional red typically observed above 
Japan3,4 (Fig. 1). This study aims to investigate the cause of this magenta aurora through photographs from the 
public, spacecraft observations, and physics-based and statistical modeling.
Utilizing citizen scientists to observe the aurora is a powerful and relatively recent advance in our field
8,9.

storm10, which was confined to the northernmost parts of Japan, with an order of 10·s of citizen observations. 
During the May 10-11th 2024 storm, 100·s of citizen observations were made across the full length of Japan 
(Method). To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest number of auroral sightings above Japan during a 
single event.

the real-time Dst index of -412 nT. This was the largest storm since the 2003 Halloween storms. When combine
with a favorable local time and slow recovery phase; this provided Japan with the right conditions to observe 
the aurorae11. The solar wind parameters, storm evolution, and citizen science observations are illustrated in

During large geomagnetic storms, red auroras are typically observed from low-latitude countries such 
as Japan. The color arises from a specific emission line of oxygen atoms at high altitudes. However, 
during the May 10-11th 2024 superstorm, magenta auroras were observed above Japan instead of 
the typical red. In this study, we demonstrate that the magenta hue is created by a mixture of red 
(O) and a blue (N
2
+) aurora at extremely high altitudes. The blue color originates from the N
2
+ first 
negative emission band caused by both resonant scattering of the upwelling molecular ions and heavy 
particle precipitation during the storm. This study is primarily driven by observations from citizen 
scientists, and confirmed and quantified with observations from spacecraft and modeling techniques. 
Additionally, we show that high solar activity, terrestrial season, and the preheating of the atmosphere 
all contribute to the occurrence of magenta aurora. This study showcases the value and richness of 
citizen science, and we anticipate that such approaches will become increasingly important in the 
future.
In early May 2024, a series of solar flares and subsequent coronal mass ejections (CME) triggered an extreme 
geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic 
Observatory and 6th in the 66-year history of the Dst index. This super storm caused aurora to appear above lo
latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time 
auroral observations on social media platforms such as X. In Japan alone, over a thousand people attempted to
view the aurora, leading to one of the densest observation efforts in the world. The public used commercially 
available cameras to capture the faint auroras that were mostly invisible to the naked eye. Remarkably, the 
photographs reveal a clear and dominant magenta hue instead of the traditional red typically observed above

During large geomagnetic storms, red auroras are typically observed from low-latitude countries such 
as Japan. The color arises from a specific emission line of oxygen atoms at high altitudes. However, 
during the May 10-11th 2024 superstorm, magenta auroras were observed above Japan instead of 
the typical red. In this study, we demonstrate that the magenta hue is created by a mixture of red 
(O) and a blue (N
2
+) aurora at extremely high altitudes. The blue color originates from the N
2
+ first 
negative emission band caused by both resonant scattering of the upwelling molecular ions and heavy 
particle precipitation during the storm. This study is primarily driven by observations from citizen 
scientists, and confirmed and quantified with observations from spacecraft and modeling techniques. 
Additionally, we show that high solar activity, terrestrial season, and the preheating of the atmosphere 
all contribute to the occurrence of magenta aurora. This study showcases the value and richness of 
citizen science, and we anticipate that such approaches will become increasingly important in the 
future.
In early May 2024, a series of solar flares and subsequent coronal mass ejections (CME) triggered an extreme 
geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic 
Observatory and 6th in the 66-year history of the Dst index. This super storm caused aurora to appear above lo
latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time 
auroral observations on social media platforms such as X. In Japan alone, over a thousand people attempted to
view the aurora, leading to one of the densest observation efforts in the world. The public used commercially 
available cameras to capture the faint auroras that were mostly invisible to the naked eye. Remarkably, the 
photographs reveal a clear and dominant magenta hue instead of the traditional red typically observed above 
Japan3,4 (Fig. 1). This study aims to investigate the cause of this magenta aurora through photographs from the 
public, spacecraft observations, and physics-based and statistical modeling.
Utilizing citizen scientists to observe the aurora is a powerful and relatively recent advance in our field
8,9. 
Such an approach was used to quantify the unusually bright auroras observed during the December 1st 2023 
storm10, which was confined to the northernmost parts of Japan, with an order of 10·s of citizen observations. 
During the May 10-11th 2024 storm, 100·s of citizen observations were made across the full length of Japan 
(Method). To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest number of auroral sightings above Japan during a 
single event.

possibly more, halo CMEs left the Sun and headed towards Earth. After reaching Earth on May 10th, an extrem

the real-time Dst index of -412 nT. This was the largest storm since the 2003 Halloween storms. When combine
with a favorable local time and slow recovery phase; this provided Japan with the right conditions to observe 
the aurorae11. The solar wind parameters, storm evolution, and citizen science observations are illustrated in 
Extended Data Figure 1.

2

2
+ first

geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic

latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time

During large geomagnetic storms, red auroras are typically observed from low-latitude countries such 
as Japan. The color arises from a specific emission line of oxygen atoms at high altitudes. However, 
during the May 10-11th 2024 superstorm, magenta auroras were observed above Japan instead of 
the typical red. In this study, we demonstrate that the magenta hue is created by a mixture of red

Additionally, we show that high solar activity, terrestrial season, and the preheating of the atmosphere

In early May 2024, a series of solar flares and subsequent coronal mass ejections (CME) triggered an extreme 
geomagnetic storm. The 10-11th May 2024 storm ranks 9th in the 110-year history of the Kakioka Magnetic 
Observatory and 6th in the 66-year history of the Dst index. This super storm caused aurora to appear above lo
latitudes countries such as Japan. Many people worldwide took great interest in the storm, providing real-time 
auroral observations on social media platforms such as X. In Japan alone, over a thousand people attempted to
view the aurora, leading to one of the densest observation efforts in the world. The public used commercially 
available cameras to capture the faint auroras that were mostly invisible to the naked eye. Remarkably, the 
photographs reveal a clear and dominant magenta hue instead of the traditional red typically observed above 
Japan3,4 (Fig. 1). This study aims to investigate the cause of this magenta aurora through photographs from the 
public, spacecraft observations, and physics-based and statistical modeling.
Utilizing citizen scientists to observe the aurora is a powerful and relatively recent advance in our field
8,9. 
Such an approach was used to quantify the unusually bright auroras observed during the December 1st 2023 
storm10, which was confined to the northernmost parts of Japan, with an order of 10·s of citizen observations. 
During the May 10-11th 2024 storm, 100·s of citizen observations were made across the full length of Japan 
(Method). To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest number of auroral sightings above Japan during a 
single event.
